newsitem.title: USA: Clinton appeals Whitewater ruling to Supreme Court.
newsitem.headline: Clinton appeals Whitewater ruling to Supreme Court.

text.p: The White House on Monday told the U.S. Supreme Court that it should not be forced to turn over notes of conversations between government lawyers and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton about the Whitewater affair.

Lawyers representing the office of the presidency asked the justices to overturn a U.S. appeals court ruling that the attorney-client privilege does not apply to the notes subpoenaed by Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr.

The appeal sets the stage for a legal confrontation before the nation's highest court over the authority of the White House to withhold certain information demanded as part of Starr's criminal investigation.

President and Mrs. Clinton have not been accused of any wrongdoing in Starr's long-running investigation into the Whitewater affair, a complex web of Arkansas business deals involving the Clintons and allegations of coverup.

One set of notes was based on what Mrs. Clinton told White House lawyers about her grand jury testimony on Jan. 26, 1996, when she said she did not know how Whitewater-related legal billing records ended up in the White House residence.

Another set of notes, dated July 11, 1995, concerned her activities immediately after the July 1993 suicide of deputy White House counsel Vince Foster, who worked with Mrs. Clinton at the Rose Law Firm in Little Rock when her husband, President Bill Clinton, was governor of Arkansas.

The Supreme Court justices are expected to decide by the end of next month whether to grant or deny the appeal. If the appeal is granted, arguments would be scheduled during the court term that begins in October.

The White House asserted in the appeal that the long-standing legal doctrine of attorney-client privilege applied to the conversations that Mrs. Clinton had with a team of government and private lawyers.
The privilege has been recognised as protecting conversations between attorneys and their clients from disclosure on the grounds such discussion require confidentiality.

But Starr has said White House lawyers, as government employees rather than the Clintons' personal lawyers, were "duty-bound" to turn over the disputed notes. He also said the unprecedented claims of privilege by the White House had delayed his investigation for months.
In the 30-page appeal asking the justices to hear the case, lawyer Andrew Frey called the appeals court decision "unprecedented," warning that it will have "grave consequences."

Frey said it "will substantially impair the ability of the office of the president (and other federal agencies) to secure sound legal advice, particularly in the face of independent counsel investigations."

He added, "The next step will be for the grand jury to require the White House counsel or other government attorneys to testify about conversations with the president or other government officials" about legal advice and details of internal investigations.

The dispute dates back to June 21, when the subpoena was served on the White House. The court battle initially was conducted in secret, but was made public early this month when the White House said it would appeal to the Supreme Court.
The White House won the first round of the court fight but lost on appeal, setting up the fight at the Supreme Court level.
